Subject: Post-call: Acme Financial evals / next steps for model fit and dataset

Hi Emily — thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our discovery: 

Summary of needs
- Primary use case: real-time customer support summarization + intent classification across loans and payments flows.
- Quality priorities: preserve legal/financial phrasing, low hallucination on account-specific instructions, high intent/classification recall for dispute-related queries.
- Latency: target 150–300ms p50 on short queries (<= 512 tokens) for interactive UI.

Recommended approach
1) Run customer-specific evals on Redwood using your example dataset (we discussed 2k-5k labeled rows to start).
2) Evaluate 3 candidate model classes: a) smaller low-latency model (Redwood-optimized-7B-8k) for most traffic, b) medium accuracy model (Redwood-13B-q4) for higher-quality routes, c) heavy accuracy model (Llama-3-70B / 70B quantized) as fallback for high-risk workflows.
3) Scoring: exact-match for structured responses, intent F1 for classification, confusion matrix for top intents, and a hallucination check metric (ratio of unsupported assertions).

What we need from you
- Provide a sample of labeled data (jsonl: {"input":..., "reference":..., "intent":...}) — 1–2k rows preferred to start.
- Share any prompt-set you want us to test (we attached our recommended prompt-set template).

Next steps / timeline
- You: share sample dataset and any safety/PII constraints by June 4.
- Us: spin up a baseline eval run (3 models above) and share a report + benchmark links within 48 hours of dataset receipt.
- Optional: schedule a 30-min results sync after we share the report.

Attachments: acme_eval_prompt-set.jsonl (prompt templates), acme_eval_dataset_sample.jsonl (sample format), redwood_eval_template.xlsx (scoring rubric).

Let us know if that timeline works. Happy to scope down the initial run if you need a faster turn.

Best,

Hi Emily — quick technical answers: 

1) Hallucination / factuality checks
- We run an automated heuristic first: exact-match against the reference + a lightweight entailment classifier to detect unsupported assertions. That flags ~85–90% of obvious hallucinations.
- For high-confidence audits (legal / finance), we recommend sampling 200–500 rows for human review post-automated pass. We flag anything above a 2% hallucination rate for follow-up.

2) PII & retention
- For hosted evals we offer short retention (30 days by default) and option to wipe datasets after runs. For Private deployments we can enforce customer-managed KMS and no-tenancy guarantees. We'll include a short Data Processing Addendum covering this.

3) Dataset format / multi-turn guidance
- Preferred format: jsonl with top-level fields: id, input, reference, intent, metadata. For multi-turn, include an array 'turns' serialized as a single string field or use conversation prefixing in 'input'. Example attached in acme_eval_dataset_sample.jsonl.
- Recommended sample sizes: 1k for initial smoke tests, 5k for reliable per-intent metrics, 10k+ for production-grade baselines.

4) Eval mechanics & artifacts we produce
- We run the dataset across selected model variants with identical prompt-set. Outputs: per-example predictions, confidence scores, per-intent precision/recall, confusion matrix, and a regression delta report vs our Redwood baseline. We host results on a run URL and can provide CSV/xlsx artifacts.

5) Quick note on model choices
- If latency is critical, Redwood-optimized-7B-8k is usually the best cost/latency tradeoff. For legal phrasing retention we see significant lift on the 13B+ quantized family. We'll include benchmark links with the run.

Links: benchmark report https://docs.redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme-finserv-eval-report-2026-05; example run https://redwood.app/runs/ev-90821.

Attachment: eval_run_instructions.pdf (scripts + CLI commands), redwood_eval_template.xlsx (scoring rubric).
